notes.b: Digestion is the breakdown of large food molecules into small soluble ones that can pass through the wall of the small intestine into the blood. It is chemical digestion, carried out by enzymes through a reaction called hydrolysis.
points: Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts, which means they speed up digestion without being used up.
Each enzyme has an active site (the part where the food molecule binds) whose shape fits one type of substrate (the molecule the enzyme acts on), so an enzyme acts on only one kind of molecule.
Enzymes lower the activation energy of a reaction (the energy needed to get it started), so digestion proceeds at body temperature, about 37 °C.

Each digestive enzyme has an optimum pH, the acidity at which it works best: pepsin works in strong acid, while pancreatic and intestinal enzymes work in the alkaline conditions of the small intestine.
Hydrolysis breaks a chemical bond by adding water: a hydrogen atom attaches to one part of the molecule and a hydroxyl group (–OH) to the other.
Protein is a chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, so proteases (also called proteinases), the enzymes that digest protein, work by hydrolysing these bonds.

As protein is digested the chains get shorter in this order: protein, then peptones (shorter chains), then peptides (shorter again), then amino acids. Only amino acids, and the very smallest peptides, are small enough to absorb.
Diagram: two amino acids joined by a peptide bond, with the water molecule added during hydrolysis labelled.
notes.tip: Learn the order protein, peptones, peptides, amino acids as one chain. Marks in the table question go for exact words, so peptones and peptides must never be swapped.

notes.h: Protein digestion table (organ, secretion, enzyme, substrate, product)
notes.b: Examiners ask you to fill in this table, so learn each row as a set of five linked words. The substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts on and the product is what it is turned into.
points: Stomach: gastric juice; pepsin; protein; peptones.
Stomach of infants: gastric juice; rennin; caseinogen; casein.
Pancreas (its enzyme acts in the duodenum): pancreatic juice; trypsin (a proteinase); peptones; peptides.
Small intestine: intestinal juice; peptidases (also called erepsin); peptides; amino acids.
notes.tip: Pepsin acts on protein and makes peptones; trypsin acts on peptones and makes peptides. Students swap them. Always name the organ and the secretion as well as the enzyme, learn substrate and product as a pair, and remember the pancreatic enzyme works in the duodenum, not in the pancreas. For the Ordinary Level fill-in, learn two sentences: rennin changes caseinogen to casein in the stomach, and trypsin from the pancreas changes peptones to peptides in the duodenum.

notes.h: Mouth and stomach: protein digestion begins
notes.b: Protein digestion starts in the stomach, not the mouth. The stomach uses acid to prepare the protein and then an enzyme to start splitting it.
points: In the mouth no protein is digested, because saliva contains no protein-digesting enzyme. Chewing breaks food into pieces and so increases its surface area, but this is mechanical only.
Gastric glands in the stomach wall secrete gastric juice, which contains hydrochloric acid and the inactive enzyme pepsinogen.
Hydrochloric acid unfolds (denatures) the protein, exposing its peptide bonds to enzyme action. Acid also kills most bacteria in food.
Hydrochloric acid converts pepsinogen into the active enzyme pepsin, and also gives the acid pH of about 2 that pepsin works best at.
Pepsin hydrolyses protein into peptones, which are shorter chains than the original protein.
Protein-digesting enzymes are themselves proteins, so pepsinogen is made inactive and activated only in the stomach. This is why it does not digest the cells that make it.
Rennin, found in the stomach of infants, clots milk by changing the soluble milk protein caseinogen into insoluble casein (curds), so milk stays in the stomach long enough for pepsin to act on it.
The stomach churns food into chyme, a semi-liquid mixture that passes slowly into the duodenum (the first part of the small intestine).
notes.tip: Rennin changes caseinogen (soluble) to casein (insoluble) in infants. Do not say it digests lactose or that it is the same as pepsin.

notes.h: Small intestine: protein digestion is completed
notes.b: Peptones leaving the stomach are still too large to absorb. In the small intestine two more enzymes, one from the pancreas and one from the intestinal wall, finish the job.
points: The pancreas is a gland, not part of the alimentary canal (the tube food passes through), so food never enters it. It secretes pancreatic juice into the duodenum through the pancreatic duct.
Pancreatic juice contains trypsin, which is made in inactive form as trypsinogen so that it cannot digest the cells that make it.
Enterokinase, an enzyme from the lining of the small intestine found in the intestinal juice, converts trypsinogen into active trypsin.
Pancreatic juice is alkaline because it also contains alkaline salts, so it neutralises the acid chyme and gives trypsin the working pH it needs.
Trypsin hydrolyses peptones into shorter peptides, which are still too large to be absorbed.
Intestinal juice is secreted by glands in the wall of the small intestine and contains peptidases (erepsin).
Peptidases hydrolyse peptides into amino acids, the main form in which protein is absorbed. Protein digestion is now complete.
notes.tip: The pancreas is a gland, so name the duodenum as the place where trypsin works. Bile is not a protein-digesting secretion and has no enzymes, so never give it in a protein table.

notes.b: Trace the journey of protein from mouth to liver in order, naming the organ, secretion, enzyme, substrate and product at each stage, then how the products are absorbed.
points: Mouth: no protein is digested, because saliva contains no protein-digesting enzyme.
Stomach: pepsin acts on the protein (and rennin in infants), and chyme passes into the duodenum.
Duodenum: trypsin and then peptidases complete digestion, and pancreatic juice enters through the pancreatic duct.
Villi of the small intestine: amino acids are absorbed into the capillaries (the tiniest blood vessels) inside each villus.
The capillaries join to form the hepatic portal vein, which carries the absorbed amino acids from the small intestine to the liver.
Liver: processes the amino acids before they enter the general circulation.
Diagram: the digestive system, labelled mouth, oesophagus, stomach, liver, pancreas, small intestine, large intestine and hepatic portal vein, with where protein digestion begins and ends marked.
notes.tip: For a longer answer, name the organ and the secretion as well as the enzyme at each stage, include the acid's roles in the stomach, and finish with absorption. Name the villi and the hepatic portal vein, never just a vein.

notes.b: Absorption is the passage of digested nutrients through the wall of the small intestine into the blood or lymph. The small intestine is built to make this fast.
points: The small intestine is long, and its lining is folded into villi, finger-like projections whose cells have microvilli (tiny folds on their surface), so the surface area for absorption is very large.
Each villus has a thin one-cell-thick wall, so nutrients have only a short distance to cross, a capillary network, and a central lacteal (a lymph vessel).
Amino acids are absorbed mainly by active transport, which uses energy and carrier proteins and is coupled with the uptake of sodium ions.
Amino acids move through the cells lining each villus into the capillary network inside it. They do not enter the lacteal, which is the route for fat.
Very small peptides (two or three amino acids) may be absorbed too. They are broken down into amino acids inside the cells.
Diagram: cross-section of a villus showing the capillary network, lacteal, epithelial wall (the one-cell-thick lining) and microvilli.
notes.tip: Amino acids go to the liver by the hepatic portal vein, not by the lacteal. In a product box write amino acids, not peptides.

notes.h: Utilisation of amino acids (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Once absorbed, amino acids are used where the body needs them. The body has no store of amino acids, so any not needed are broken down in the liver.
points: Body cells take up amino acids from the blood and use them to build body protein for growth and repair, and to make enzymes, hormones and antibodies.
The liver makes plasma proteins, such as albumin, from amino acids and passes the rest on in the blood.
Amino acids cannot be stored, so surplus amino acids are broken down in the liver.

Deamination is the removal of the amino group (–NH₂) from an amino acid. In the liver it is converted to ammonia (a nitrogen-containing compound formed when the amino group is removed from an amino acid), and then to urea because ammonia is toxic.
Urea is carried in the blood to the kidneys, filtered out and excreted in urine.
The remaining carbon part, with its carboxyl group (–COOH), is oxidised to release heat and energy, or converted into glucose or fat. This is why protein is an energy source when eaten in excess.
notes.tip: Deamination is the breakdown of excess amino acids, so do not confuse it with digestion or with making body protein. Do not call ammonia the final excretory product: it is turned to urea first. Marks go for the uses of amino acids, plasma proteins made by the liver, and deamination to urea.

keyTerms.definition: The splitting of a chemical bond by adding water, giving two smaller molecules.
The chemical bond that links two amino acids in a protein chain.
The active gastric enzyme that hydrolyses protein into peptones, activated by hydrochloric acid.
The pancreatic protease that hydrolyses peptones into peptides in the small intestine.
An enzyme in intestinal juice that converts inactive trypsinogen into active trypsin.
A finger-like projection of the small intestine wall that absorbs digested food through its capillaries and lacteal.
The blood vessel that carries absorbed nutrients from the small intestine to the liver.
The removal of the amino group from an amino acid in the liver, producing ammonia.

factCards.term: Four functions of hydrochloric acid in the stomach
factCards.definition: It unfolds protein so enzymes can act on it, converts pepsinogen into pepsin, provides the acidic pH pepsin needs, and kills most bacteria in food.

factCards.term: What activates the inactive pancreatic protease in the small intestine
factCards.definition: Enterokinase, found in the intestinal juice, converts trypsinogen into trypsin.
Pepsin acts on protein as its substrate and produces peptones as its product.

factCards.term: Where rennin acts and what it changes
factCards.definition: Rennin acts in the stomach of infants, changing caseinogen into casein, which clots milk.

factCards.term: Two structures that increase absorptive surface in the small intestine
factCards.definition: Villi, the finger-like projections of the intestine wall, and microvilli on the surface of the cells lining each villus.

factCards.term: Blood vessel carrying absorbed amino acids from the villi to the liver
Nitrogen-containing compound formed when the amino group is removed from an amino acid

questions.prompt: Outline the digestion of dietary protein in the stomach and in the small intestine. For each organ, name the secretion, the enzyme, the substrate and the product.
questions.model: Stomach: gastric juice from the stomach wall. Hydrochloric acid converts pepsinogen into pepsin. Pepsin acts on protein, the substrate, to produce peptones. Small intestine: pancreatic juice from the pancreas. Trypsin, activated from trypsinogen by enterokinase in the intestinal juice, acts on peptones to produce peptides. Peptidases in the intestinal juice hydrolyse peptides into amino acids.

questions.prompt: Trace the route of dietary protein from the mouth to the liver. Explain how protein is hydrolysed at each stage, how the products are absorbed, and what the liver does with the amino acids it receives.
questions.model: Mouth: no protein digestion, as saliva has no protein-digesting enzyme. Stomach: hydrochloric acid unfolds protein and activates pepsin, which hydrolyses protein to peptones; rennin changes caseinogen to casein in infants. Duodenum: pancreatic juice contains trypsin, activated by enterokinase, which hydrolyses peptones to peptides; intestinal juice peptidases hydrolyse peptides to amino acids. Absorption: villi increase the surface area; amino acids are absorbed mainly by active transport coupled with sodium ions into the capillaries of the villi. Hepatic portal vein carries the amino acids to the liver. Liver: amino acids are used to synthesise plasma proteins; surplus amino acids are deaminated, removing the amino group, which forms ammonia that is converted to urea; the carbon skeleton is used for energy or converted to glucose or fat; urea is filtered by the kidneys and excreted in urine.
